tips.title: Two different percentages
tips.body: **Percentage yield** measures how much product you actually got compared with the most you could have got. **Atom economy** measures how much of the starting material ends up as the product you wanted. One is about the practical run; the other is fixed by the equation alone.

tips.title: Yield is actual over theoretical
tips.body: $$\% \text{ yield} = \frac{\text{mass actually made}}{\text{maximum theoretical mass}} \times 100$$ The theoretical mass is what a reacting-mass calculation predicts. If your yield comes out above 100%, the product is still wet or you have divided the wrong way round.

tips.title: Atom economy uses the equation, not the experiment
tips.body: Atom economy needs **no measurements at all** — only the balanced equation. Add up the $M_r$ of **every** reactant, divide the $M_r$ of the product you want, and multiply by 100. The same reaction always has the same atom economy however well or badly it is run.

tips.title: One product means 100%
tips.body: If a reaction makes **only one product**, every atom that went in comes out in it, so the atom economy is **100%**. The Haber process is the standard example. Spotting this saves the calculation entirely.

tips.title: Three reasons a yield falls short
tips.body: The reaction **may not go to completion** because it is reversible; some product is **lost when it is separated** from the mixture; and some reactants **react in other ways** to give different products. Those three are the marks — vague answers about "spillage" are not.

steps.title: Percentage yield
steps.body:
Conservation of mass says no atoms are lost, yet chemists almost never collect the full amount a calculation predicts. The **yield** is the amount of product actually obtained, and comparing it with the maximum possible gives the **percentage yield**.

$$\% \text{ yield} = \frac{\text{mass of product actually made}}{\text{maximum theoretical mass of product}} \times 100$$

**Why it is never 100% in practice.** AQA lists three reasons, and they are the ones a mark scheme credits:

- **The reaction may not go to completion**, because it is **reversible** — some product turns back into reactants.
- **Some product is lost when it is separated** from the reaction mixture — left in the filter paper, on the glassware, or in the solution.
- **Some reactants react in ways different to the expected reaction**, producing something else instead.

**A high yield is not the same as a fast reaction, or a cheap one.** A reaction can be quick and still give a poor yield, and vice versa.

**A yield above 100% is impossible** and always means an error: usually the product was weighed while still damp, so the mass includes solvent, or the division was done the wrong way up.

steps.title: Atom economy
steps.body:
A reaction can have a fine yield and still be wasteful, because much of what went in ends up as **by-products** you did not want. **Atom economy** measures how much of the starting material becomes the useful product.

$$\% \text{ atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of the desired product from the equation}}{\text{sum of the } M_r \text{ of all reactants from the equation}} \times 100$$

**It comes from the equation alone.** No measurements, no yield, no conditions — the same reaction always has the same atom economy.

**Worked for lime from limestone**, $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$, wanting the calcium oxide:

$$\frac{56}{100} \times 100 = 56\%$$

The other $44\%$ leaves as carbon dioxide.

**Worked for iron from its ore**, $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 3\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_2}$:

- wanted: $2 \times 56 = 112$
- all reactants: $160 + (3 \times 28) = 244$
- $\dfrac{112}{244} \times 100 = 45.9\%$

**Why it matters.** High atom economy means less waste to dispose of, less raw material used per tonne of product, and lower cost — so it is central to **sustainable development**.

**One product means 100%.** In the Haber process, $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, the reactants total $34$ and the ammonia is $34$ — identical, so the atom economy is **100%**.

steps.title: Choosing a reaction pathway
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

Industry often has **more than one route** to the same product, and choosing between them means weighing several things at once. AQA asks you to justify a choice given data, and the factors are:

- **Atom economy** — how much of the raw material ends up as useful product.
- **Percentage yield** — how much is actually obtained in practice.
- **Rate** — a route that is slow ties up the plant and costs money.
- **Equilibrium position** — for a reversible reaction, how far it goes before it stops.
- **Usefulness of the by-products** — a low atom economy matters far less if the by-product can be **sold** rather than disposed of.

**No single number decides it.** A route with 90% atom economy but a terrible rate may be worse than one at 60% that runs quickly. A route whose by-product is a saleable chemical effectively recovers much of the waste.

**Answering these questions well** means naming the factor, quoting the figure, and saying what it implies:

> *Route A has the higher atom economy (85% against 40%), so less raw material is wasted per tonne. However, Route B has a much higher yield and its by-product is sold as fertiliser, so the waste from B has value. Given the cost of disposing of A's waste, B may be preferable.*

That is a **comparison with a conclusion**, which is what the marks are for — not a list of numbers.

steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write the formula for percentage yield.
2. Write the formula for atom economy.
3. Give the three reasons a yield is less than 100%.

**Part B.**

4. A reaction should give 40 g and 32 g is collected. Find the percentage yield.

**Part C.**

8. Explain why a yield of 105% must be wrong, and give the most likely cause.
9. Two routes make the same product. Route A: atom economy 90%, yield 40%, very slow. Route B: atom economy 55%, yield 95%, fast, by-product sold as fertiliser. Recommend one, with reasons.

For question 9, a recommendation without a reason earns nothing.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep the two percentages apart.** Yield is about **this run** of the reaction; atom economy is about **the equation**. A question asking why a reaction is wasteful even at 100% yield is testing exactly that distinction — the answer is that the by-products still carry away atoms.

**Calculate the theoretical mass properly.** It is a reacting-mass calculation from the **limiting** reactant, not just the mass you started with. Dividing the actual mass by the reactant mass is a common and costly slip.

**Divide the right way round.** Actual over theoretical. A yield above 100% is impossible, and the usual cause is **weighing a product that is not yet dry**, so the mass includes water.

**Use the equation's coefficients in atom economy.** For $2\mathrm{Fe}$ the mass is $2 \times 56 = 112$, not $56$; and **all** reactants go on the bottom, including the ones that seem minor.

**Spot the 100% case instantly.** One product means nothing is wasted. It is worth checking before starting the arithmetic.

**Link atom economy to sustainability explicitly.** Less waste to dispose of, fewer finite raw materials consumed per tonne, lower energy and cost. "It is better for the environment" alone is too vague.

**Weigh factors against each other.** The top band wants a **judgement**: name the factors, quote the figures, and say which wins and why. A route with a saleable by-product can beat one with better atom economy.

**Remember that a reversible reaction caps the yield.** If a question mentions equilibrium, the reason the yield is low is that the reaction does not go to completion, not that the chemist was careless.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- $\% \text{ yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{theoretical mass}} \times 100$.
- The **theoretical mass** comes from a reacting-mass calculation.
- Yield falls short because the reaction is **reversible**, product is **lost on separation**, or **side reactions** occur.
- A yield over **100%** is impossible — usually a wet product.
- $\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{total } M_r \text{ of all reactants}} \times 100$.
- Atom economy comes from the **equation alone**, and never changes for a given reaction.
- Use the **balancing numbers**: $2\mathrm{Fe}$ is $112$, not $56$.
- **One product → 100% atom economy**, as in the Haber process.
- Lime from limestone is **56%**; iron from its ore is **45.9%**.
- High atom economy means **less waste**, fewer raw materials and lower cost — it supports **sustainable development**.
- *(HT)* Choosing a route weighs **atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium position and the usefulness of by-products**.
- A **saleable by-product** offsets a low atom economy.

questions.solution: In a reversible reaction the products **react back** to re-form the reactants. The reaction therefore settles at an equilibrium with both present, and **never goes to completion**, so some reactant always remains unconverted and the yield stays below 100%.

questions.prompt:
Iron is extracted by Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which has an atom economy of 45.9%. Ammonia is made by N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, which has an atom economy of 100% but a percentage yield of only about 15% under the conditions used.

Compare the two processes, explaining what each measure tells you and why a high atom economy does not by itself make a process efficient. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
**Atom economy** is calculated from the balanced equation alone and never changes for a given reaction. It measures what proportion of the atoms in the reactants end up in the product you want. For iron, $\dfrac{112}{244} \times 100 = 45.9\%$, so **more than half** of the mass of the reactants leaves as carbon dioxide, which must be dealt with and represents wasted raw material.

**Percentage yield** measures a particular run: the mass actually obtained against the maximum the equation allows. It is reduced by reversibility, by losses during separation and by side reactions.

The Haber process shows why the two must be read together. Its atom economy is **100%** — ammonia is the only product, so no atoms are wasted at all — yet its yield is low, about 15%, because the reaction is **reversible** and reaches equilibrium before completion. A single pass converts little of the gas.

However, the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are **recycled** back through the reactor, so almost all of them are eventually converted. That makes the low yield far less damaging than it first appears, and overall the Haber process wastes much less raw material than iron extraction does. A high atom economy alone does not make a process efficient, and a low yield alone does not make one wasteful — the two, together with rate and what happens to the by-products, decide it.

examTechnique.body:
Keep the two measures apart: **yield** is actual over theoretical for a particular run; **atom economy** comes from the equation and never changes.

For a yield question, calculate the **theoretical mass** first with a reacting-mass calculation, then divide the actual mass by it. For atom economy, use the **balancing numbers** and put **every** reactant on the bottom. When asked to choose a route, name the factors, quote the figures and give a judgement.
examinerErrors: Treating yield and atom economy as the same measure.
Dividing the actual mass by the mass of reactant instead of the theoretical mass.
Accepting a yield above 100% instead of identifying a wet product.
Ignoring the balancing numbers in atom economy.
Leaving a reactant out of the denominator.
Saying only "better for the environment" for sustainability.
Listing data without reaching a conclusion.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer separates the two measures cleanly and can say why a reaction may be wasteful at 100% yield or efficient at 15%. It builds the theoretical mass from the equation before dividing, uses the balancing numbers and every reactant in an atom economy, and spots a single-product reaction as 100% without calculating. Asked to evaluate a route, it names atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium position and the value of the by-products, quotes the figures, and commits to a conclusion — including the point that recycling unreacted gas rescues a low yield.
